CUI inspection methods compared: profile RT, PEC, guided wave and neutron backscatter side by side

Short answer: the four best-known CUI methods measure different things. Neutron backscatter (and infrared thermography) finds wet insulation, not corrosion. Guided wave UT screens long straight runs for loss of cross-section and tells you where to look. Pulsed eddy current (PEC) measures average remaining wall under a footprint through the insulation. Profile radiography images the actual wall profile and corrosion product. A sound programme screens with the fast methods, confirms with RT or with direct UT and visual examination at stripped windows, and lets the owner's inspector decide where insulation comes off.

This section adds a method-by-method comparison, guidance on matching methods to components, the workflow from screening to confirmation, and the records an API 510 or API 570 inspector expects. It complements the overview above and the CUI inspection service page. No method here replaces the inspector's judgement or the owner's CUI programme, and vendor performance claims vary: qualify any method on representative mock-ups before relying on it.

The comparison table: what each method actually measures

The single most useful question to ask of any CUI technique is "what physical quantity does it measure?" The answer decides what a "clean" result means and what follow-up is needed.

MethodWhat it measuresOutputCoverage styleKey limitsTypical follow-up
Neutron backscatterHydrogen in the insulation, i.e. water (and hydrocarbons)Wet/dry map along the lineFast scanning of jacketed lines and vesselsNo metal-loss information; radioactive source needs licensing and controls; hydrogen-bearing insulation materials can confuse readingsPEC, RT or stripped-window UT at wet zones
Infrared thermographySurface temperature differences on the jacket caused by wet insulationThermal imagesVery large areas, including from a distanceNeeds a temperature difference between process and ambient; weather, sun and jacket emissivity affect results; no metal-loss informationNeutron backscatter or thickness method at anomalies
Guided wave UTChanges in pipe cross-section that reflect a low-frequency guided waveReflector locations and estimated cross-section change along the pipeLong straight runs from a single collar positionRange drops with bends, supports, coatings, viscous contents and heavy corrosion; poor on small isolated pits; not a sizing methodProfile RT, PEC or UT at the indicated location
Pulsed eddy currentAverage wall thickness of ferromagnetic steel under the probe footprintGrid of percentage or absolute wall valuesPoint-by-point grids through insulation and jacketingFootprint averaging under-calls small pits; metal mesh, steel jacketing and nearby geometry reduce accuracy; cannot separate internal from external lossProfile RT or UT at low readings
Profile radiography (film, CR or DR)Silhouette of the wall at the tangent of the pipe, plus image of corrosion product and scaleRadiographic images with measured wall at tangent pointsShot-by-shot; good on small bore, elbows and supportsRadiation exclusion zones and licensing; limited to diameters and wall thicknesses the source and detector can penetrate; depth measured mainly at tangent pointsStrip and confirm with visual and UT where findings are significant
Real-time / digital radiography scanningSame as profile RT, viewed live as the device moves along the lineLive or recorded imagesFaster scanning of small and medium boreEquipment availability; same radiation controls; resolution varies by systemProfile RT or UT for measurement
Stripped window: visual + UTActual surface condition and thicknessPhotographs, pit depths, UT readings or mapsOnly where insulation is removedCost of removal, reinstatement and, on older systems, asbestos handlingRepair, re-coat, re-insulate; feed corrosion rates to the inspector

The table shows why combinations work. A wet-insulation map from neutron backscatter or thermography narrows down where water is; guided wave narrows down where metal has gone on long runs; PEC grids quantify average loss on shells and large pipe; profile RT shows the shape of the damage at specific locations; and direct examination at a stripped window gives the number the inspector ultimately uses.

Pulsed eddy current in more depth

PEC is popular because it needs no couplant, no surface preparation of the steel and no radiation, and it works through insulation and many jacket types. A probe induces a pulsed magnetic field; the decay of the eddy currents in the steel is related to the wall thickness. Peer-reviewed work on PEC for CUI (for example a 2023 study in the journal Materials) describes the core limitation clearly: the reading is an average over a footprint that grows with insulation thickness, so a small isolated pit can be diluted by the sound steel around it and under-reported. The same study showed that metal mesh embedded in insulation enlarges the footprint and reduces sensitivity.

Practical consequences for planning:

  • Use PEC for general or wide-area wall loss, not to prove the absence of pitting.
  • Set grid spacing deliberately. Wide spacing is fast but leaves gaps between footprints; the owner's inspector should agree the spacing for each consequence tier.
  • Treat readings near flanges, supports, nozzles and changes in diameter with caution, because nearby metal changes the response.
  • PEC gives a relative value against a calibration point; confirm the reference on a known area, ideally with UT at a window.
  • Record jacket type, insulation thickness and any mesh, because they change performance and must be repeated at the next survey for valid comparison.

Profile radiography in more depth

Profile RT places the source and detector so the beam passes tangentially through the pipe wall at the edges of the image. The steel wall appears as a band whose width can be measured, after correcting for geometric magnification. Corrosion on the outer surface under the insulation shows as a change in the wall profile and as corrosion product between the steel and the insulation. Older editions of API 570 stated that radiography or insulation removal with visual inspection is normally required at damaged or suspect CUI locations, with other NDE methods allowed where applicable; check the current edition for today's wording.

Strengths: it works on small bore, elbows, tees and pipe at supports where PEC and guided wave struggle, and the image is a permanent record that can be compared over time. Limits: wall measurement is only exact at the tangent points, so loss on the face of the pipe needs a different exposure angle or a second shot; penetration limits apply on large or thick-walled pipe; and every exposure requires radiation safety controls. In the United States, industrial radiography is licensed by the NRC or by an Agreement State radiation control programme, while in Canada gamma radiography sources are licensed by the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission and X-ray equipment falls under provincial rules. Digital detector arrays and computed radiography have shortened the time per shot and allow image enhancement, but the geometry rules are the same. See radiographic testing for the method itself.

Guided wave and neutron backscatter in more depth

Guided wave UT. A transducer ring clamped at one location sends low-frequency waves along the pipe in both directions. Reflections come from welds, supports, fittings and areas of metal loss. The method excels on long straight runs, road crossings, sleeved sections and pipe racks where access is limited, because one collar position covers a long length. Range depends heavily on the pipe: coatings, heavy general corrosion, many supports, bends and liquid contents all shorten it. It reports cross-section change, so a small deep pit can be below the detection threshold while a shallow but wide area is easy to see. Every indication needs a follow-up measurement. For long-range screening practice, see guided wave testing.

Neutron backscatter. A sealed neutron source emits fast neutrons; hydrogen atoms in water slow them, and a detector counts the slow neutrons that return. High counts mean hydrogen, and on most insulated lines that means water. The method is quick and needs no contact with the steel, which makes it a good first pass across a unit to rank lines by wetness. Its limits are inherent: it does not measure corrosion, hydrocarbon leaks into insulation also contain hydrogen, some insulation materials contain hydrogen, and the radioactive source requires licensing and controls. A dry reading is useful evidence; a wet reading is a reason to look further.

Matching methods to the component

  • Long straight runs on pipe racks: neutron backscatter or thermography to find wet zones, guided wave to screen for metal loss, then PEC or profile RT at indications.
  • Small-bore piping (roughly 2 inch and under) and tubing: profile RT or real-time radiography; PEC and guided wave are often impractical.
  • Elbows, tees and closely spaced fittings: profile RT; PEC only with probes and calibration suited to the geometry.
  • Pipe supports, clamps and shoes: profile RT and visual examination; supports are classic water traps and also hinder guided wave and PEC.
  • Vessel shells and large-diameter pipe: PEC grids, with neutron backscatter or thermography to prioritise, and windows at nozzles, rings and skirts.
  • Insulated tank shells: PEC on accessible courses, windows at the bottom course and at stiffening rings, and profile techniques at nozzles.
  • Dead legs and low points: direct examination or RT; screening methods rarely give enough confidence on short, complex configurations.
  • Austenitic stainless steel: the concern is usually external chloride stress corrosion cracking rather than wall loss, which needs insulation removal and surface methods; see the guide on chloride stress corrosion cracking.

From screening to confirmation: a defensible workflow

  1. Rank the population. The owner's CUI programme, often built with API RP 583 as guidance, groups lines and vessels by temperature range, insulation and jacket type, coating, age, environment and consequence. Our API RP 583 article covers the framework.
  2. Screen for moisture and visible damage. External visual survey of jacketing, seals, penetrations and supports; neutron backscatter or thermography where useful.
  3. Screen for metal loss. Guided wave on long runs, PEC on shells and large pipe, real-time radiography on small bore.
  4. Confirm. Profile RT and stripped-window visual and UT at the locations chosen by the inspector from the screening results, plus a share of "clean" screening locations to check that the screening is not missing damage.
  5. Record and trend. Tie every reading to a fixed reference so the next survey measures the same place, and feed confirmed thickness data into the inspector's corrosion-rate calculations.

Step 4 matters more than it looks. If insulation is only ever removed where screening found something, the programme never tests its own blind spots. Planned verification windows at locations that screened clean are the evidence that screening works on that site's insulation, jackets and pipe sizes.

What the inspector of record needs in the report

  • Method, procedure reference, equipment, calibration or reference standard, and technician certification level for each technique.
  • Exact locations referenced to line numbers, isometrics or drawings and fixed physical markers.
  • For PEC: grid spacing, footprint size at the actual insulation thickness, jacket and insulation details, and the reference location.
  • For guided wave: collar position, test range achieved, sensitivity and call levels used, and features identified.
  • For RT: technique, source or tube, detector type, magnification correction and measured wall values at each tangent.
  • For neutron backscatter or thermography: conditions at the time of survey and the threshold used to call "wet".
  • Areas not inspected and why.

With that, the owner's API 510 or API 570 inspector can compare survey to survey, set corrosion rates and decide intervals and insulation removal under the code and the owner's programme. Atlantis does not set those intervals.

Common mistakes when comparing CUI methods

  • Treating a dry neutron or thermography result as "no corrosion". It only says the insulation was dry at the time of the survey.
  • Using PEC to clear pitted areas. Footprint averaging can hide small deep pits.
  • Running guided wave through a forest of supports and bends and reporting full coverage without stating the range actually achieved.
  • Measuring profile RT wall at one tangent only when damage could be on the face of the pipe.
  • Skipping verification windows at clean screening locations.
  • Not recording insulation and jacket details, which makes later PEC surveys non-comparable.

How Atlantis supports CUI method selection and screening

Atlantis NDT performs CUI screening and confirmation NDE within the owner's programme: guided wave screening, PEC grids, profile radiography by radiography crews licensed where the work is performed, and UT thickness and corrosion mapping at stripped windows, carried out by ASNT-certified technicians under ASNT Level III oversight. The owner and its API-certified inspector choose strip locations, set intervals and accept results. Atlantis does not perform risk-based inspection or fitness-for-service assessments. More questions about CUI inspection methods

What is the best NDT method for corrosion under insulation?

There is no single best method. Profile radiography and stripped-window UT give the most direct evidence; PEC, guided wave and neutron backscatter are faster screening tools. Most programmes combine them.

Can pulsed eddy current detect pitting under insulation?

Only partly. PEC averages wall thickness over its footprint, so small isolated pits can be under-reported. It is best for general wall loss and for deciding where to look more closely.

Does neutron backscatter detect corrosion?

No. It detects hydrogen, which on insulated lines usually means water in the insulation. It shows where CUI is likely, not whether metal has been lost.

Is guided wave testing good for CUI?

For long straight runs, yes, as a screening tool. Bends, supports, coatings and heavy corrosion shorten its range, and it cannot size individual pits, so indications need follow-up.

Why is profile radiography used for CUI?

It shows the actual wall profile and corrosion product through the insulation, works on small bore and fittings, and leaves a permanent image for comparison at the next inspection.

Do you still need to remove insulation if screening is clean?

Usually some verification windows are still needed, because every screening method has blind spots. The number and location are decided by the owner's inspector and CUI programme.
